newsitem.title: CANADA: Toronto exchange seen driving to 6,000 in year.
newsitem.headline: Toronto exchange seen driving to 6,000 in year.

text.p: Despite hitting new highs every session last week, the Toronto Stock Exchange, Canada's largest, has nowhere to go but up as the improving Canadian economy lures foreign investors, analysts said.

The Toronto Stock Exchange's key 300 Composite Index is expected to surpass 5,600 by year end after ending last Friday at an all-time high of 5,287.47 and could hit 6,000 points within a year, analysts said.

"I would see this market continuing on its merry way past the (U.S.) election, certainly in the first part of next year, before there might become a rather longer period of market consolidation," ScotiaMcLeod Senior Vice-President Fred Ketchen said. The U.S. election is on Nov. 5.

The TSE 300 Index has lagged the growth on New York's Dow Jones Industrial Average this past year. The Dow jumped from 4,793 points a year earlier to close at 5889 points on Friday after setting a record of 5,889.20 on Monday.
A year ago the TSE 300 Index was around 4,377.

Canada's strengthening economy is giving foreign investors more reasons to invest in Toronto stocks, which are heavily weighted in favor of gold mining companies and other natural resources, said HSBC James Capel Canada strategist Bob Boaz.
Natural resource firms see higher production during economic revivals that increase earnings.

"Now you're starting to see the Canadian economy perform almost as well as, actually as well as the U.S. economy," Boaz said. "We've probably seen that international flow of funds start to come into Canadian stocks."
Independent analyst Josef Schacter forecast the TSE 300 Index will reach 5,400 points by November.

Schacter said the index could hit 5,600 by year end, aided by the recent news that Canada's quarterly current account swung into surplus for the first time in more than a decade. The current account is a measure of a country's balance of payments with the rest of the world.
The growing U.S. economy sucked in Canadian goods while imports fell, which could help cut the government's foreign borrowing as it generates its own cash.

"I think foreign interest will be there because our balance of payments will be in better shape, our interest rate structure is in good shape and of course we'll be providing a lot of product to the U.S. market," Schacter said. Canada's short-term interest rates have dropped 4.0 percent since May 1995.
"All of that is part of the ingredients for a strong export-related sector, which will drive corporate profits," Schacter said.
Ketchen added that dividend-bearing equities will remain popular with foreign and domestic investors, while Canadian bonds provide comparatively low returns.
"Rates of return on the fixed income side are relatively minimal when you compare them to what you can at least receive on first grade Canadian securities of an income nature," he said.
"I still think we're heading still up and I think we have lots more room to move," Ketchen said.

Boaz added that "my belief is that as long as interest rates stay reasonably stable at this point and even if you get a ... sideways motion in the New York market, it still allows the TSE to move to higher levels," Boaz said.

Ketchen said that the long-awaited resurgence in Canadian consumer confidence could help boost the economy. "Canadians will catch up on some of their lack of spending that they have had over the past and we will find that consumers will start to untighten the buttons on their pockets."
